source.title: How Optimality Structures Sparse Dictionaries: A Theory for Understanding SAE Representations

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and empirically checks first-order optimality constraints on SAE reconstruction residuals. This bears on whether residual structure is shaped by the dictionary-learning objective, but it does not use the dark-matter study’s measurements or test its specific predictability and scaling claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports residual-condition measurements in section 5 and Appendix D.6; these are included below. Its other SAE results concern feature-feature constraints, dataset shifts, dense features and width limits, not the listed claim versions. Values from cited work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper derives first-order optimality conditions for vanilla dictionary learning and checks whether real SAE residuals satisfy them, using the residual break ratio λ*/λtrain. This measure asks whether residual directions are consistent with the L1 objective at the training strength. It does not measure how large the dark matter is or whether it is linearly predictable. It also does not test whether the error shrinks with better architectures or end-to-end training, or what the error does to the model. Its argument that the objective decides which features may stay in the residual is related to V6's framing. However, it makes no claim that dark matter is mostly a training artifact, and no result shows that. The residual measurements therefore belong under fits_no_version, not as a test of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors derive necessary first-order optimality conditions for vanilla dictionary learning. They use these to explain feature splitting and absorption, which features can remain in the residual, dense antipodal pairs, and unbounded splitting as products of the objective. They present the conditions as a cheap diagnostic: real SAEs pass on training-like data and fail increasingly on more distant data such as code, foreign-language text and distant layers.
record.recipe_differences: Uses theoretical first-order dictionary-learning optimality conditions and residual-break measurements, rather than the original dark-matter study's error-predictability, norm-scaling or model-loss tests. The theory studies vanilla dictionary learning; empirical checks use pretrained GPT2-small SAEs.
record.method_sensitivity: Residual-condition outcomes vary by dataset and test layer. The paper reports violations for code and at layer 10, but not for several other datasets and layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Residuals of GPT2-small layer-8 SAEs satisfy the feature-residual first-order optimality condition (break ratio ≤1) on OWT, C4, the Wikipedias, the Pile and nearby layers. They violate it on code data, more strongly for the 768-latent SAE, with violating features aligned to the whitespace residual PC1. The paper argues the objective constrains which structure can be left in residuals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE residual structure is constrained by the dictionary-learning objective: residual directions satisfy first-order optimality on in-distribution data and violate it under distribution shift.

record.problems: The theoretical conditions are necessary rather than sufficient. The theory is for vanilla dictionary learning rather than specific SAE encoder architectures. Empirical residual checks use GPT2-small SAEs; reported dataset results are sometimes aggregate ranges, and the joint tests are not exhaustive.
record.rows_left_out: No other residual-condition results were omitted. The paper's feature-feature tests, dense-feature toy example and ray-clustering results do not measure any listed claim version.

untested.parts: No linear prediction of the SAE error from input activations.
No per-token error-norm prediction across sizes, no overlap of failure contexts across sizes, and no test of error persisting with scale.
No comparison of downstream loss after SAE splicing against loss after random errors of the same size.
No split of the error into linear and nonlinear parts, and no test of whether either part can be learned.
No circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term.
No comparison of architectures, losses or end-to-end training, and no measure of how much dark matter remains under better training. Width sweeps report only the break ratio, not error size.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 labels are dropped. The break ratio measures objective-consistency of residual directions, not the size or origin of dark matter, so it cannot support or limit V6. The reader's own V6 'supports' reason already concedes it does not bear on the training-artifact claim. The layer-shift rows mostly pass (layers 4–9), so they did not justify 'limits_scope' either. The original dark-matter paper is not cited in the text. Preprint; code released.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure how much of the error vector can be linearly predicted from the input activation.
Does not test predictability of per-token error norms across SAE sizes, overlap of failures across sizes, or whether error vanishes with scale.
Does not compare model loss after SAE reconstruction with loss after random errors of the same size.
Does not separate error into linearly predictable and nonlinear parts, test whether either part is learnable, or compare their qualitative character.
Does not measure loss of model behaviour in circuits or steering when the error term is omitted.

Tests whether residuals satisfy constraints implied by the dictionary-learning objective across datasets and layers. Does not compare SAE architectures, end-to-end training, or establish whether dark matter mostly reflects training artifacts rather than model structure.

relation.reason: The study discusses and analyzes residual structure but neither tests the specified dark-matter claims nor uses them as a tool.

tranche.reason: The residual-break diagnostic measures consistency with dictionary-learning optimality, rather than any claim version's error predictability, scaling, functional impact, decomposition, or reduction through improved training.

source_check.notes: The diagnostic checks each feature against the top 50 residual principal directions; passing these necessary conditions does not establish full optimality. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased, subject to their stated vanilla-dictionary-learning and restricted-testing limitations.

statements.correction: OWT, C4 and English/German/French Wikipedia: ratios 0.19–0.35 at every width; Pile: 0.45–0.81; test layers 4/6/7/9: 0.78/0.70/0.63/0.52; test layer 10: ratio 17, FVU 1.38; code: overall 1.0–1.9, with main-SAE violations of 1–5% in 4 features.
statements.problem: The nearby-layer summary needs explicit scope: the cited layer-10 result has ratio 17 and reconstruction failure.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Layer-8 SAE on OWT and the listed nearby or related datasets, across the reported widths; also the Pile
reader_labels.reason: Residual break ratios are below the stated threshold of 1, so these residuals satisfy the measured condition implied by the dictionary-learning objective (r1–r2). This supports objective-consistency in these settings, not the broader claim that dark matter mostly reflects training artifacts.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Code datasets and the layer-shift tests
reader_labels.reason: The code results include ratios above the threshold, while layers 4, 6, 7 and 9 remain below it and layer 10 has a large ratio where reconstruction fails; the measured residual behavior depends on dataset and layer (r3–r9).
